title: {{NAME}} and the Match Nobody Believed Could Happen
moral: Fairness matters more than victory, and choosing it takes more courage than any goal.

pages.content:
The Pangaea Pitch was the oldest and most famous sports ground in the known world: a vast oval of emerald grass carved into the basin of an ancient meteor crater, its terraced walls draped in the flags of every team that had ever played there. Today, every seat was filled. The noise was a physical thing, a warm pressing wave that {{NAME}} felt in the sternum before hearing it with the ears.

The Dino-Rangers were the home team: four Velociraptors of remarkable agility, a Triceratops defender named Tres whose three horns had accidentally deflected more goals than any intentional save in league history, and {{NAME}}, the newest and smallest member, whose superhero speed had earned a starting spot in the biggest match of the season. Opposite, in their midnight-black kits, were the Storm Wolves: seven human players, every one of them fast, skilled, and currently eyeing the pitch with the calm confidence of a team that had never lost at Pangaea.

What nobody in the stadium knew yet was what {{NAME}} had seen while warming up. One of the Storm Wolves, their brilliant striker, had tucked something into their boot. Small and metallic, barely visible. A movement amplifier: a device that was very much against the rules and would give the wearer a sprint advantage no one could match. {{NAME}} pressed both hands together. This was going to be complicated.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} could have said nothing. The amplifier would have been hard to prove in the heat of a match. The Storm Wolves would probably win anyway, and {{NAME}}'s team would lose with dignity and that would be the end of it.

But that was not what the suit was for. The scarlet fabric and the white lightning bolt were not decorations. They meant something about the kind of person who chose to wear them.

At the pre-match handshake, {{NAME}} pulled the Storm Wolves captain, a tall young woman named Sable, aside from the line. 'Your striker has a movement amplifier in the left boot,' {{NAME}} said, low and direct. 'If the referee finds it during a match, your whole team gets disqualified. Your season is over.' Sable's expression went through several complicated changes, like a weather system passing over a mountain. 'Why are you telling me this instead of the referee?' she asked. Her eyes were sharp and careful. {{NAME}} met them steadily. 'Because I want to win against your actual team, not against a disqualification.'

Sable was quiet for a very long moment. Then she walked back to her players. A brief, tense conversation. The striker bent down, removed something from the boot, and dropped it in the recycling bin by the corner flag. The crowd, who had noticed nothing, roared as both teams took the field.

pages.content:
The match that followed was the finest either team had ever played.

With no unfair advantage in play, the Storm Wolves were exactly as good as their reputation: fluid, disciplined, fast. Sable orchestrated the midfield like a conductor directing an orchestra that had memorised every piece. She was wonderful to watch, even when she was making {{NAME}}'s life difficult, which she did constantly.

The Velociraptors on the Dino-Rangers were in extraordinary form, their quick clawed turns leaving opposing players spinning and confused. Tres anchored the defence like a small geological feature, immovable and reliable, accidentally using one horn to redirect a storm-wolf shot onto his own teammate's shin, which was unfortunate but somehow the ball ended up exactly where the Rangers needed it.

{{NAME}} scored in the seventy-third minute, a sprint down the right channel at full superhero speed, a cross clipped to exactly the height where the Velociraptor striker called Zip was waiting, and Zip's overhead kick, which was technically very difficult for a creature with such short arms, somehow connected and somehow flew true. The net filled. The stadium erupted. Tres bellowed with all three nostrils. {{NAME}} ran to Zip and they collided at full speed and fell over, which was fine because the grass was soft and the score was one-nil and neither of them had intended to be dignified about it.

pages.content:
The Storm Wolves equalised in the eighty-ninth minute, a Sable free kick of such perfectly calculated curve it seemed to bend the laws of geometry. One-one. Extra time.

The stadium had never been louder. The meteor crater amplified sound in a way its ancient builders could not have predicted, and fifty thousand voices in it became something beyond noise, a force, a tide. {{NAME}} could feel it in every muscle.

In the third minute of extra time, {{NAME}} had a clear run on goal, a burst of full speed, VALT-level focus. Then Sable went down hard on the wet grass beside the box, clutching her ankle. No foul had been committed. It was simply the match being difficult, as matches are.

Everyone expected {{NAME}} to keep running. The goal was open. The crowd surged forward. Tres bellowed encouragement. The Velociraptors shrieked.

{{NAME}} stopped and helped Sable to her feet. In the four seconds that took, the defensive cover came back. The opportunity closed. The match went to penalties.

Sable, still limping slightly, lined up and took the first penalty for the Storm Wolves. She placed it with absolute precision and scored. She looked at {{NAME}} before she walked back. It was the same look {{NAME}} had given her at the handshake: steady, and worth something.

pages.content:
The penalties went to six rounds each, which was unprecedented and which sent three members of the crowd to the medical tent with palpitations. Tres converted his with a cautious tap that barely crossed the line and which the crowd treated as the most dramatic moment in sporting history.

Zip's final penalty was the decisive one, placed with absolute conviction in the top-left corner, and when the net shook, the Pangaea Pitch made a sound that the seismologists in the next province recorded as a small but measurable event.

Sable found {{NAME}} in the celebratory chaos and shook hands properly, with both hands, which meant something in the old tradition. 'Best match I've ever played,' she said. She meant it. {{NAME}} thought that was worth more than the trophy, but accepted the trophy too because it was also extremely good.

Later, much later, {{NAME}} sat in the quiet corner of the changing room with the trophy between both knees and let the evening's sounds fade to something comfortable and distant. Tres was snoring outside with tremendous enthusiasm. Zip was still doing victory backflips, alone, in the car park.

Close your eyes now. Let the crowd noise become the sound of wind in the leaves. Let the floodlights fade to stars. And when you sleep, dream of what it felt like to run, and to stop, and to know the difference between the two.
